label: EmArcy
rationale: Dinah Washington is the largest vocal absence left in the canon: 341 albums and not one by the singer they called the Queen, who was the bridge from the blues shouters to the jazz-and-R&B singers who came after her. This is the record to start with, and it is a canon pick on the listing traditions rather than a token: NPR's Basic Jazz Record Library recommends it outright (S6), AllMusic rates it five stars and files it under vocal jazz and standards (S2), the Encyclopedia of Popular Music gives it five and the Penguin Guide three and a half (both recorded in S1). Session gravity is the strongest part of the case - it is not a singer with a pickup band but the actual 1954 Max Roach-Clifford Brown working band (Brown, Harold Land, Richie Powell, George Morrow, Roach) plus Clark Terry, Maynard Ferguson, Herb Geller, Junior Mance and Keter Betts, ten heavyweights on one date, taped live in front of a studio audience that producer Bob Shad deliberately brought in (S2, S6). A.B. Spellman's NPR description is exactly the rubric's discovery test: 'a jam session in the purest sense ... loose, live, and just fun to listen to' (S6). It also documents what a blowing session sounded like at the moment hard bop was forming - Brown's obbligato on 'No More', Land's tenor on 'Darn That Dream', Geller's alto on 'Crazy He Calls Me' (S2) - and every one of those players except Dinah herself is already in the canon, so the record adds edges as well as a voice. Honest caveats: the repertoire is entirely standards and show tunes, with no originals; it is a vocal date in a canon centred on instrumental post-bebop; AllMusic's own style tags are Vocal Jazz, Standards, Traditional Pop and Classic Female Blues, not bop (S2). Style is coded bebop for the improvisational idiom and to match the canon's own convention for jazz-vocal records (Ella in Berlin and Betty Carter's The Audience are both bebop), with the vocal-jazz framing recorded here rather than hidden.

personnel_record.notes: One session, 15 August 1954, taped live before an invited studio audience in Los Angeles (S1, S2, S6); AllMusic gives the recording location only as 'Los Angeles, CA' and no source names the room, so the session is placed at the canonical city-level row los-angeles-venue-unidentified rather than at an invented studio. Producer Bob Shad is named by Wikipedia and by NPR, which credits him with bringing in the live audience (S1, S6). No engineer is credited on any source consulted - the original EmArcy credits, AllMusic, Discogs and Wikipedia are all silent - so engineer is null rather than inferred. Recording year 1954 is used as the album year per the canon convention, although the LP was released in February 1955 on EmArcy MG 36000 (S1, S3, S5). The original 12-inch programme is eight tracks (S5); the 11-track edition on Apple, Discogs and Wikipedia adds 'Darn That Dream', 'Crazy He Calls Me' and 'I'll Remember April', flagged here as bonus tracks (S1, S2, S3). Personnel is the date roster, all ten musicians on the single session; per-track distribution among the two pianists and two bassists is not documented anywhere consulted, and track personnel arrays are therefore marked inf and track_assignments_complete is false. Wikipedia's track note that 'Alone Together' and 'Summertime' are instrumentals is followed, so Dinah Washington is recorded as absent from those two tracks (S1); that note is the only per-track personnel statement in the sources.

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded in 1954 and first released in 1955, both within the window; its vocal-jazz/standards identity intersects with bebop and early hard-bop improvisation, but neither reference considers this a scope barrier.

ballot.case_for: NPR's Basic Jazz Record Library explicitly recommends the album (S6), and AllMusic awards five stars (S2), providing direct support beyond Washington's historical stature. The Brown–Roach working-band nucleus, augmented by Clark Terry, Maynard Ferguson, Herb Geller and others, places her blues-rooted phrasing inside a consequential mid-1950s improvising ensemble rather than a conventional singer-with-accompaniment setting (S2, S6). Brown's obbligato on 'No More' and the invited-audience spontaneity make the session gravity audible, while NPR's description of a loose, live, enjoyable jam directly supports the discovery test. It offers a compelling introduction to a major vocalist absent from this canon without relying on representation alone.
ballot.case_against: The strongest objection is whether an expansive, deliberately informal blowing session is Washington's defining album, rather than an outstanding shared showcase: she is absent from two of the original eight selections, and ensemble display competes with sustained vocal interpretation (S1). The dossier establishes exceptional participants and critical enthusiasm more clearly than album-specific influence or a uniquely coherent artistic conception. Consensus also needs qualification: the Penguin and Encyclopedia ratings are reported indirectly through Wikipedia, and two highlighted performances belong to the expanded edition rather than the original LP (S1–S5). Incomplete piano and bass assignments warrant sessionographical caution, though they do not themselves diminish the music.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 judges the recommendation history, session gravity and importance of Washington's absence sufficient for consensus_core/must_have; Reference 2 judges it contested/strong because the jam-session format and divided vocal/instrumental identity leave its status as her definitive statement open to challenge. Both accept its scope and musical distinction; their genuine split concerns canonical necessity and album-level definition.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give Dinah Jams strong consideration through listening, distinguishing the original eight-track album from the expanded edition before deciding whether it is his defining Washington selection.
